items.q: How big is tonight's blue tide compared with every red and blue tide of the last 50 years, measured the same way?
items.a: Measured as the change in the Democratic margin of the House vote from the previous election: tonight, across the 138 districts on unchanged lines that are at least half counted, Democrats are +15.4 where the same districts were R+2.2 in 2024, a swing of +17.6 points. Nothing since 1976 matches it on the blue side: 2006 was +10.6, 2018 +9.7, 1982 +9.5. The only swing of this size in either direction was the 2010 red wave, −17.4; 1994 was −12.2. Caveat: tonight's number is an early count (59% of those districts' 2024 vote) and early-counted mail and early ballots lean Democratic in most of these states, so expect it to come down as Election Day ballots are added; the historical bars are final national House margins. The lab re-measures it every five minutes.

items.q: when was the last time we had a Dem gov in Tx
items.a: Ann Richards, elected in 1990 and in office from January 1991 to January 1995; she lost the 1994 race to George W. Bush. Every governor since has been a Republican: Bush (1995–2000), Rick Perry (2000–2015) and Greg Abbott (2015–present), 31 years and counting. The drought is wider than the governorship: no Democrat has won any statewide office in Texas since 1994. Tonight Gina Hinojosa leads Abbott 55–45 with about two-thirds of the expected vote counted (as of 7:07pm; the race is not called), which would make her the first Democratic governor since Richards.

items.q: What is the current breakdown of seats in the house and senate
items.a: Going into tonight Republicans hold the House 218 to 214, with one independent and two vacant seats; 218 is a majority, so Democrats need a net gain of only a few seats. Republicans hold the Senate 53 to 47 (45 Democrats plus 2 independents who vote with them), and Vice President Vance breaks ties. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot tonight; Republicans are defending 22 of those Senate seats, Democrats 13.

items.q: How many House seats does the president's party usually lose in a midterm? (the long view)
items.a: Since 1946 the president's party has lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms, about 26 seats on average. The only gains were 1998 under Clinton (+4) and 2002 under George W. Bush (+8). The biggest losses were 2010 under Obama (-63), 1946 under Truman (-56) and 1994 under Clinton (-54); 2022 under Biden was a small one at -9.

items.q: Show me a graph of how much the presidents party typically suffers in the midterms.
items.a: The president's party lost ground in both recent midterms. The Republicans lost about 4.8 points of the two-party House vote from 2016 to 2018 under Trump, and the Democrats lost about 2.8 points from 2020 to 2022 under Biden. These figures come from the national House vote in our data, which only goes back to 2016, so the chart shows two midterms and not a long-run average. No results are in yet tonight, so nothing from 2026 is on the chart. When the count starts, the early numbers will be partial, and big blue counties often count more slowly.

items.q: How has nationwide turnout in House races changed over the last five elections?
items.a: House races drew about 128 million votes in 2016, 113 million in 2018, 153 million in 2020, 107 million in 2022 and 148 million in 2024. Midterms run well below presidential years: 2018, the highest-turnout midterm in about a century, still came in 15 million votes under 2016, and 2022 drew about 41 million fewer House votes than 2024. The question tonight is whether 2026 lands closer to 2018 or to 2022.
